analysis.one_liner: Rolls back federal bans on offshore and federal-land oil leasing and fast-tracks new oil refinery permits.
analysis.headline: The bill to open federal lands to oil drilling and speed refinery permits was introduced in July 2008 and never received a House vote before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out every federal law that blocks leasing federal offshore waters, Bureau of Land Management land, National Forests, and oil shale lands for oil, gas, and oil shale development. When oil traded above $100 a barrel, it would require the Interior Secretary to waive federal drilling permit requirements outright. It would also put the Energy Department in charge of refinery permits, set strict deadlines for federal and state agencies, and let the Energy Secretary hand out approvals itself if an agency missed the deadline. It was proposed during the 2008 gas-price spike as a response to pump prices above $4 a gallon.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to federal offshore, western land, and oil shale reserves currently off-limits to leasing, and would face fewer federal drilling permits and faster refinery approvals. The bill's own findings cite an estimated 88 billion barrels in the Outer Continental Shelf and over a trillion barrels of oil shale, most of it on federal land. Drivers might eventually see some price relief, though new drilling and refining capacity takes years to come online and most independent analyses found the effect on pump prices in the near term was small.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies and drillers

how_it_helps.text: Declares all federal laws prohibiting leasing of federal offshore, Bureau of Land Management, National Forest, and submerged lands for oil, gas, or oil shale to have no force or effect.
Requires the Interior Secretary to waive federal drilling permit requirements whenever West Texas Intermediate crude trades above $100 a barrel, and permits waivers below that price.

Makes the Department of Energy the lead agency for refinery permitting, lets it set binding deadlines for federal and state agencies, and requires automatic approval within 30 days if an agency misses the deadline.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the public would bear the cost of losing environmental review protections on federal lands and waters, since agencies could not slow or stop projects that missed the Energy Secretary's deadlines. Communities near new refineries would absorb local environmental impacts without the normal hearing process. Environmental protections that applied for decades would be bypassed rather than repealed by their own terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, local communities, and the environment

drawbacks.text: The automatic waiver provision removes environmental and safety reviews whenever oil prices are high, which is precisely when drillers have the most incentive to cut corners and when public lands face the heaviest pressure.

Under the refinery provisions, state agencies acting under federal delegated authority could have their permit decisions overridden by the Energy Secretary if they missed a federally imposed deadline, undercutting state-level environmental control.

New drilling and refining capacity takes years to bring online, so the bill would not deliver quick relief at the pump despite its emergency framing; its findings acknowledge an offshore platform takes roughly seven years and $5 billion before producing oil.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is aimed at a real problem, record gasoline prices in 2008, and expanding supply is a legitimate policy response. But its specific design replaces ordinary environmental review with an automatic price trigger and a hard deadline that defaults to approval, meaning the burden shifts onto the public and local communities whenever agencies cannot move fast enough. The bill also conflates long-run supply with short-run price relief, so its own findings undercut the urgency of its remedies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in July 2008, sent to subcommittees, and never reached the House floor before Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 31, 2008, during a period when gasoline averaged $4.07 a gallon, according to the bill's own findings.

It was referred to the Committees on Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Agriculture, then to subcommittees on Energy and Air Quality, Energy and Mineral Resources, and Department Operations, Oversight, Nutrition and Forestry.
No further action was taken after October 3, 2008, and the bill never received a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Environmental and land-protection interests, and ordinary people who benefit from keeping federal lands and waters under ordinary leasing rules, benefited from the bill going nowhere, as did any communities that would have hosted fast-tracked refineries without full review. Oil and gas companies did not gain the expanded access the bill would have provided, though it should be noted some OCS restrictions were later lifted by other means.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Environmental protections held; drillers gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would end federal leasing bans on offshore and western federal lands and waive drilling permit requirements when oil prices are high, handing drillers access to reserves they currently cannot reach. The cost falls on the public in the form of lost environmental review on shared lands and waters.

Refiners would get a new fast-track path to construction permits with automatic approval if agencies miss deadlines, cutting years and local opposition out of the process. Refiners benefit from looser rules even though their product, gasoline, is what drivers buy.

The bill terminates federal restrictions on oil shale leasing, opening a resource the bill says is concentrated on federal land in Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming. This is currently off-limits to commercial leasing programs.
